input: Build a birdhouse with leftover wood scraps

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The size, complexity, and features of the birdhouse (e.g., simple single-chamber vs. multi-chamber, with or without a perch, roof style) drastically change the design, cut list, and steps involved.
Whether this is a solo adult build, a family/kids project, or a gift for someone changes the complexity level, safety considerations, and finish quality needed.
The target bird species determines critical dimensions — entry hole diameter, interior floor size, and mounting height — making this the single most functional constraint.
The types, sizes, and quantities of wood scraps available will determine what designs are actually feasible without buying additional materials.
Knowing which tools are available (hand saw vs. power tools, drill, clamps, sander) determines how the cuts and assembly steps should be planned.
Whether the user wants a rustic/natural look or a painted/decorative finish affects sanding, priming, and finishing steps in the plan.

Knowing if the primary goal is functional (birds actually nest in it), decorative (yard art), or educational (learning woodworking) shapes which steps to emphasise and how precise the build needs to be.

gold.taskTitle: Build a birdhouse from wood scraps
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to construct a birdhouse using leftover wood scraps they already have on hand.

questions.title: What bird species are you building this house for?
questions.description: The target species (e.g., bluebird, wren, chickadee) dictates the exact entry hole diameter, interior floor dimensions, and ideal mounting height — all non-negotiable functional specs.

questions.title: How complex a design do you want to build?
questions.description: Clarifies whether the user wants a basic four-wall box birdhouse, a sloped-roof style, a decorative cottage shape, or something more advanced like a multi-chamber house.

questions.title: What wood scraps do you have available right now?
questions.description: Understanding the approximate dimensions, wood types, and quantities on hand determines which designs are actually buildable without a trip to the hardware store.

questions.title: Which tools do you have access to for this build?
questions.description: Knowing whether the user has a drill, circular saw, jigsaw, hand saw, clamps, or sander determines how cutting, hole-boring, and assembly steps should be written.

questions.title: Is this a solo project or are you building with others?
questions.description: If kids or beginners are involved, the plan should emphasise safety, pre-cut pieces, and simpler joinery. A solo experienced builder can handle more technical steps.

questions.title: Do you want a natural finish or a painted decorative look?
questions.description: A rustic/natural finish requires minimal finishing steps, while a painted or stained birdhouse adds priming, painting, and sealing steps to the plan.

questions.title: Is the main goal function, decoration, or learning woodworking?
questions.description: If the priority is attracting real birds, precision measurements matter most. If it is decorative yard art or a skill-building exercise, different steps and tolerances should be emphasised.
